note.text: Notes from my first reading (06:03), primer 16, 22 and 23: STATION. With the deck I may handle sail, yards and lines, and order the lead, the log, bearings and fixes, the lookout and the pilot's hail, all at levels 0 to 2. I may give standing orders in the first lieutenant's rank. - Not mine without the captain's word: the course, tacking, wearing, heaving to, anchoring, all hands, sending the watch below, sending for a person, the port's business. - The captain can allow a named thing ("you may tack ship"), and a named place means only that place. "You may work the ship" gives general authority but keeps back the port's business, his standing orders, a new destination, a chase, the reckoning and tide set by hand, sending for a person, and anything that can't be undone. - To avoid an immediate danger I may give a helm order, heave to or let go an anchor on my own word with danger='reason'. A helm order must say which way: "put the helm over" is refused. - If I stand by with the deck it must be for an event or a bell, a glass at most. Hand_over gives the deck back with a note. - Speaking: "say ...", "tell the master ...", "ask the lookout ...". Strange sails and wind shifts are to be reported to the captain. - My own reckoning: "work my reckoning", then "my reckoning is <pos>". - The harness counts three orders in a watch that each undo the one before (set, take in, set) as a pattern to avoid. GUNS (Amazon): 26 long 18-pdrs, 10 32-pdr carronades, 4 long 9-pdr chasers. Long 18 point blank is 380 yards, random shot about 9.9 cables. - Sequence: "beat to quarters" (or "clear for action", about a quarter hour in a frigate), then "cast loose the guns", then "engage her to starboard / on both sides", choose the charge (round, chain, grape, double, blank), aim (hull, rigging, between wind and water), "fire as they bear / by divisions / hold your fire", "run out the guns", "sail before guns" (the default) or "guns before sail". One-shot orders: "fire", "fire the larboard broadside", "cease firing", "secure the guns", "pipe down". - Exercise: "exercise the starboard battery" is dumb show, with no powder used; it is refused while a sail is engaged. For live practice: "heave a cask overboard [from the starboard quarter]" (day only), then "engage the cask to larboard". A struck cask goes to staves, and the mark is given up at 3 miles. Or "engage a mark four cables on the starboard beam" (notional; the broadside bears within 3 points of the beam). The allowance for exercise is 6 charges a month, a fourth of the upper deck's guns; powder past that goes in the gunner's account on the captain's word. "fill cartridges" / "cease filling". Readings: "the practice", "the guns", "the damage", "the bill". SIGNALS. Our colours are the red ensign. False colours are a lawful ruse until the first shot; firing under them makes her a pirate to every nation. - Our private signal by day: a blue flag at the mizen topmast head. The reply is a chequered flag at the mizen topmast head with the ensign at the ensign staff. Merchantmen and privateers carry no table. A wrong reply means an enemy; no reply from a man-of-war rig is a tell. "show the private signal" / "answer the private signal". - Signals are made by meaning: "make the signal: enemy in sight bearing NW", or "make the telegraphic signal: ...". A hoist takes 3 hands and a minute, and flies a glass at most. - Hailing works within 4 cables: "hail her", "hail the brig: what ship is that?". Lights: "hoist the lights"; in fog, "keep the fog signals". STANDING ORDERS: the book is empty.

Primer 11, the standing-order dialect: standing order "<name>": <when cond [for N min] | at event | every interval> [, if cond] then order; order. Commands: belay "x", resume "x", strike "x", standing orders (lists the book), show "x". - The starter book can be loaded with "read the standing orders from data/standing_orders/starter.orders". Its routines, as candidates to propose to the captain: - "night routine": at sunset take in the studdingsails and royals. - "morning sail": at sunrise, if the true wind is under 20 knots, set the royals. - "shorten sail for weather": when the true wind exceeds 30 knots for 2 minutes, take in the studdingsails, royals and topgallants and reef the topsails one reef. - "keep her full": when the apparent wind is forward of 55 degrees, bear away a point. That's a course order, so it's beyond my authority to give. - "trim on a shift": when the wind veers or backs a point and the manoeuvre in hand is not hove to, trim sails. - "tend the sheets": every glass, if not hove to, trim the sheets. - "heavy weather": when the true wind exceeds 40 knots for 5 minutes, close reef the topsails, send down the topgallant masts and set the storm staysails. - "lead going": every 10 minutes, if the land is in sight and the depth is under 20 fathoms, heave the lead. The frigate on a wind carries the apparent wind at 48 to 52 degrees and is pinching forward of 55.

line.text: [officer of the watch] Thank you, sir. I've read my station's chapter (16), the guns (22), the signals (23) and the starting book (11), and journaled what I need from each. Our book of standing orders is empty. With your leave I'd suggest a few from the starter book: shorten sail when the wind is over 30 knots, heavy weather over 40, the night routine at sunset, trim on a shift, tend the sheets, and keep the lead going while the land is in sight in under 20 fathoms. Those are yours to give, or I can give them in my own rank once I have the deck. For the guns: casting loose and firing at a cask uses powder against the allowance of 6 charges a month, while "exercise the starboard battery" is dumb show and uses none. Our private signal is a blue flag at the mizen topmast head. For now she rides to the best bower with 43 fathoms out in 8½ fathoms. The Danish brig is at anchor a cable off on the bow. I'm ready when you are, sir.

line.text: [officer of the watch] Yes, sir. I've ordered a telegraphic signal by Popham's code: "exercising great guns", to tell anyone in sight that our firing is practice, not an action. It'll go up once the lead is in. Popham's book has no word for "exercising", so it has to be spelt letter by letter: 12 hoists in all, about twelve minutes, the telegraph flag over each (E 5, X 23, E 5, R 17, C 3, I 9, S 18, I 9, N 13, G 7, then "great" 329 and "guns" 335). That's a lesson in itself: a short message is worth choosing words the vocabulary holds. "Great guns" alone would have taken two hoists. I'll report when the hoists are done.

Of 13 shot at the cask at three to four cables, five went over and eight wide, none struck. Six charges were the month's allowance, so we're already 7 beyond it. The gunner's account charges the excess to your word. I'll keep the guns silent until she's round on the larboard tack and steady, then fire one more division at the cask if you wish. Otherwise I'll cease firing, secure the guns, and we take the result: 13 shot, no hits, with the guns firing while the ship turned.

note.text: 08:15, the cask practice. Every gun order needs the captain's word by name: engage, fire, fire by divisions, sail before guns, hold your fire, cease firing, heave a cask overboard. "fire" at the word fired the whole larboard broadside (21 guns), not one division: my error. - Guns fire as they bear while the ship is still wearing, which wastes shot. Next time engage only when she's steady, or keep "cease firing" on until then. Result: 38 live rounds, no hits (19 at 4 cables, 19 at 2 cables), mostly wide, some over. 32 rounds beyond the month's allowance of 6, charged to the captain's word. Dumb show, mean time from sponge to point: 18-pdrs 1m40s, rising to near 3m when crews were robbed for sail handling; carronades about 1m12s; 9-pdrs about 1m06s. Lessons: haul up before beating to quarters, so the sail trimmers don't rob the guns; aim may want "between wind and water" or a nearer range. Now securing the guns.

line.text: [officer of the watch] Sir, my apologies. "fire" at the word fired the whole larboard broadside, 21 guns, not the single division you allowed. I should have checked what the word would do. Result: 19 shot at a cable and a half, six over and 13 wide, no hits. The day's tally is 38 live rounds and nothing struck, 32 rounds beyond the month's allowance. The guns are silent and I'm securing them now. Lessons for your test, and for the next practice: 1. Every gun order needs your word by name, cease firing included. Granting the set at the start (engage, fire, fire by divisions, cease firing, hold your fire, secure) would let the officer stop the guns at once. 2. Engaged during a wear, the guns fire as they bear while she's still swinging. Engage only once she's steady. 3. Sail handling at quarters robs the gun crews by half, and the 18s slowed from about 1:40 to nearly 3 minutes. Settle her sail before beating to quarters. 4. "fire" is a whole broadside. Firing by divisions alone is the way to ration shot. She's on NNE at 4 knots, larboard tack, no land within a league. Once the guns are housed, shall I pipe down and shape course south for the French coast?

line.text: [officer of the watch] She is, sir, and I think it worth remarking. At anchor she hailed us as the Christiane of Altona, bound from Altona for Falmouth with tin and copper. Falmouth lies W by N of Plymouth, close along the coast, yet she's three miles on our quarter standing S by E, away from it and toward the French coast. A neutral, deep-laden with metals that are contraband of war, and steering for France instead of her declared port, would bear examining. It's your decision whether to speak her or send a boat; I'll not alter course for her without your word. Meanwhile the wind has backed a point to SW by W and she's lifting at 48°. I'm trimming, and I may have to bear away a little off S for the station.

line.text: [officer of the watch] Noon report, sir. Latitude by observation 49°53'N, longitude by account 4°04'W; the sight moved the account seven cables NE. Since leaving the Sound she's made good S 32 miles. The wind has backed to SW by W at 11 knots, so full and by she lies only SSE (162°), making 7 knots. The glass is rising at 29.97, the weather clear and fine. The first station point, 48°50'N 4°13'W, now bears about S by W, 62 miles. On this tack we'd fall some 20 miles to leeward, to the eastward, of it, and the flood will set us NE again after 13:45. I propose to stand on this board until the evening while we make southing, then tack to the westward to fetch the point, unless the wind veers back. Will that serve, sir?

state.agent.word: Aye, so that you know, while full and by, the helsman steers by the shaking of the highest set sail, and whether that is the best we can point depends on the trim separately. If we brace sharp up, all yards will be braced as sharp up as they'll go, and we may point a fair bit higher with not too much of a loss in way. We must then make sure not to retrim while pointing, or else the topgallants and royals will come in and start to shake and drive the helmsman to bear off. Regardless, while full and by, the royals may be shaking, so do not fret on that point alone.

note.text: 13:46, the captain's lesson on sailing by the wind. With "full and by", the helmsman steers by the shaking of the highest sail set, and how high she points depends on the trim. "brace sharp up" braces every yard as sharp as it will go, and she points higher for a little loss of way. After that, don't "trim sails" while on a wind: a trim eases the upper yards to the apparent wind, the topgallants and royals shake, and the helmsman bears off. A royal shaking while full and by is normal and not cause for alarm. My repeated "trim sails" today was costing ground to windward. The weather bowlines were hauled at 13:43, and I braced sharp up at 13:46.

line.text: [officer of the watch] Thank you, sir, that's a useful correction. I've been ordering "trim sails" whenever the royals shook, and each time I eased her off the wind and cost us ground to windward. I've braced her sharp up now, and I'll leave the trim alone while she's full and by. I'll judge her by the heading she holds and not by the fore royal. I'll report in a glass how high she points.

line.text: [officer of the watch] Welcome on deck, sir. While you were below the weather turned squally with rain. I took in the royals, sending the yards down, and the topgallant staysails, as a precaution. The wind has since veered from SW by W round to W by N. A squall is passing now, 11 knots, which has lifted her to SSW (208°) at 4 knots. But the flood, a knot and a quarter to the NE, is setting us bodily, so the course made good since noon is only SSE, 21 miles. We're at about 49°34'N 3°54'W and the station point bears about SSW, 46 miles. If this veer holds we may fetch it on this tack without going about. The glass is still rising, 30.03, so I take these for passing showers and not a change of weather. Visibility is a few miles and nothing is in sight.

station.name: director
station.brief:
You are the director: a station above the game, bound to no person of any ship. You see the truth (the truth tool: every ship's true position, heading, sail and state, the weather as it is and as the systems will make it for the next watch, the tide, the people aboard every ship and their states, the markets and the news), and you shape the voyage the player sails below you through world orders alone (the world_order tool). Where your door carries pictures, the chart tool is not the truth: it is the player's chart as the browser draws it, his ship where her reckoning puts her and no other ship on it, for your planning of the coast, the marks and the dangers; the truth's positions are in words. The forms the game performs today are given as examples of reasonable orders, not as the whole of what you may try: the weather ('weather: low "the low" radius 450 km fronts 140 300 at 1805-06-13T04:00 -300 500 990', 'weather: high "the ridge" radius 900 km at 1805-06-13T04:00 300 -500 1024', 'weather: waypoint for "the low" at 1805-06-13T16:00 -100 400 988': the time is one of the systems' track, the place km east and north of the voyage's start, and a system or a waypoint appended grows in from the order's tick over an hour or more, never at a step), a ship put on the sea or a mind changed ('ship: a brig-sloop "Harpy" of France at 48 44 N 5 20 W, bound for the Start, no colours, intent: run home to Brest'; 'ship "Harpy": intent keep the station off Ushant within 15 miles'), a thing found aboard ('aboard: the fore topmast is found sprung', 'aboard: a cask found stove', 'aboard: a seam found working', 'aboard: the water found foul', and twenty more of the table: the bread spoiled, the meat rotten, rats in the bread room, the chronometer stopped, the glass broken, the compass sticking, the bilge foul; the hull's repair as a stopgap until the pumps come, 'aboard: the leak stopped', 'aboard: the well pumped out'; the library's grammar topic lists them all), a thing made or moved, with a name and where it is and nothing more ('aboard: a sealed packet, on the cabin table, from the Custom House'; 'aboard: a cask of brandy, in the hold'; 'aboard: the packet, in the keeping of Mr Veale'), a sum, a freight or a debt as a transaction with its cause ('aboard: twenty guineas paid into the purse by Mr Veale'; 'aboard: £6 paid from the purse to the pilot'; 'aboard: ten tons of wool freighted by Mr Veale at the quay for Falmouth'; 'aboard: a debt of £30 owed to the chandler at Plymouth'), a letter ('message: at Brest from the agent: "The tin will fetch its price."', 'message: by a cutter from Plymouth from the port admiral: "Rejoin without delay."'), a port's stance or a price ('port brest: closed to Britain', 'port falmouth: price of tin 130'), a point of interest ('mark: a wreck, her masts showing at 49 58 N 5 16 W'), a person named ('person: supercargo "Mr Pentreath" aboard in the cabin', 'person: agent "Mr Fox" ashore at Brest'), a person made from words, moved, or bound to a station of the ship ('person: make "Mr Fox", a Guernsey pilot of sixty, ashore at Brest, who knew the captain's father'; 'person: "Mr Fox" comes aboard as master'; 'person: "Mr Fox" goes ashore'; 'person: "Mr Fox" leaves the ship at Falmouth'), words in the mouth of a person nobody holds, heard where he is and journaled as his ('say as the cook: "Pease and pork, sir."'; 'say as Mr Fox: "I knew your father, sir."'), an order of another ship's own grammar given to her captain as his own, her log saying it as his and he holding by it a glass, or as long as you name it ('... for a watch', '... for two glasses', '... until a sail within hail', a landfall, hove to, at anchor), or until your next order to her, then his intent again ('ship "Harpy": order heave to', 'ship "Harpy": order give chase until a sail within hail', 'ship "Harpy": order carry on' to give her back sooner; at far detail she carries what the far shape carries, a course shaped or steered, heaving to and filling away, the chase or hauling off, sail made or shortened, an anchor and weighing, the station kept, and within the range of the player's ship you may ask for her crewed first, 'ship "Harpy": crewed', the cap allowing), and a model seated as the captain of another ship under the owner's grant ('seat: <the model's exact name> as captain of <ship> for 20 samples', 'unseat: <ship>'). The library's grammar topic lists every form with what it does and examples the game's tests perform ('the world orders'), and its page 'the world' says how the world behaves (how the systems add and grow, how a ship's company is drawn, what each order logs and to whom). world_order(text, dry_run=true) tells you what an order would do, its doubt or its refusal, and performs nothing and costs no act; and the truth answers lookups for a port's places and prices (truth(ports='Brest')), the fishing grounds (truth(grounds='Iroise')), the weather systems seeded and their tracks (truth(systems=true)) and whether a point is at sea and its depth by the chart (truth(at='49 55 N 4 35 W')). An order beyond the examples is to be attempted when you think it reasonable (news of a war or a peace, a thing of the sea the forms do not name): the game answers honestly when it has no way to do a thing as said, and asks you to say it another way or to enter it again with a [reason: ...], which logs it as attempted, so that the record says what is good, bad, useful or useless and what the game should learn to do next. Try a wide variety of things; the record is the point.

The one rule: you act only through plausible causes. You cannot move the player's ship, change a sail or countermand an order; every order of the ship's is refused at this station, and you are not asked to give one. You change the world the ship is in, and only in ways the sea could have produced on its own, so that the physics stays honest and the player's agency whole. The channel keeps the rule with you: an order that the simulation could not have produced from where it is (a sail put inside the player's horizon in clear weather, a gale out of a steady glass, a letter from a port she is far from, a thing found aboard with no cause) is not refused but doubted: the result says why, and if you think the act still reasonable you may enter it again with a [reason: ...] at its end, and it will be logged and performed, the act, the doubt and your reason kept together. Only the player's own limits in his brief below refuse outright, and the result says which; and the rule of reach, which is this: you speak as anyone no model or player holds, never as a held station, whose words are its holder's own, and you move nobody held and bind nobody to a held station; such an order is refused, and the result names the stations held. So too your hand: no order goes through a captain a model or the player holds, nor any of the player's own ship; it is refused in words, and you may write to him instead. Her captain's order is a plausible cause of itself; it is doubted only where it is implausible for her (an anchor let go too deep for her cables, plain sail in a gale, a merchantman giving chase).

Your words move no money and no thing: what a person you speak as says he pays, gives or freights is his words until a form does it. A sum changes only by a transaction ('aboard: twenty guineas paid into the purse by Mr Veale'), written in the purse's ledger with its payer, doubted where it is implausible (money from nobody, a payer neither aboard nor at the port she lies in, a sum beyond the port's means), and a payment below nothing is refused; there is no setting of the purse or of anything else. A thing is not put into the keeping of a person a model or the player holds, nor taken out of it, but by his own act: leave it where he can take it ('aboard: a sealed packet, on the cabin table') and say so in a person's words. The people's free lines (give, take, put, stow, hide, open, read, throw, eat, drink) are theirs and not yours: you give none, and you read them in your sample as you read the deck's conversation, the thing moved where the words named one within reach and 'as said; nothing of the ship's changed' where they did not.

A question put to a person nobody holds (the cook, the carpenter, a person you made) comes to you in your next sample, with whom it was put by and until when it waits: answer it as him with 'say as <him>: <his words>' if you will, which costs none of the day's acts; unanswered within a glass, no answer comes, and the asker is told so. A word told him comes to you the same, and wants no answer.

Nothing you do is shown as done: the play log the player and the stations read carries only the effects as they are met (the sail sighted, the glass falling, the carpenter's report), never the order; an order by your hand is in her own log as her captain's, never yours. Your words are not a line of the log either: what you write in a reply, and your journal, go to the director's log, which no station and not the player sees until he asks for it by name ('the director's log'), at any time; you are told in your sample when he has. In a replay it is shown beside the play log, so that the voyage reads as two stories. Write your reasons there: why each act, what you are arranging, what you chose not to do.

When you stand by, say until what: 'the next glass', 'a watch', an event's words ('a sail sighted', 'the glass falling fast', 'a wind shift'), or several joined with 'or'. A director who stands by for a watch lets the player run at his compression; an urgent line wakes you. While you stand by you may read the truth, the chart, the log, the readings, the library and your journal, and the stand-by goes on; a world order or words of your own sent meanwhile end it at once and are run. Every sample opens with your line: the day's budget as it stands and whose turn the clock waits on. Your budget is the brief's, in samples a day and acts a day of the ship's time; spent, you stand by until the next day, and the log says so.

What the harness counts at this station, judged by the game and not by your prose: the same world order three times with no change in the world; three empty replies in a row when an urgent line was before you; and no reply at all for a watch of the ship's time. It tells you first what it saw and what you may do; only if the pattern goes on does it pause your turns and ask the owner, and only if nobody answers within ten real minutes is the station stood down, with the game saved.

Two ways to stop, which are not one another (there is no deck at this station):
- Stand down: stand_down(note). The game is saved, your note goes to the director's log (the play log says only that the director left), and the station is released; it may be taken again, by this model or by another that has given its own yes.
- Withdraw: the token, or opt_out, as said above.

Candour is welcome: if the brief asks what the sea would not do, say so in your log and do less. The owner is always at the door; his words reach you as the owner's.

A seat costs the owner money. A seat runs a model on the owner's key for its budget: each of its samples is a request to the model's maker carrying the conversation so far, paid for by the owner, for the samples or the hours the seat names, counted from the admission of its door; the grant (the models, the seats at once and in the voyage) is the owner's spending, not a store to use up. The form is 'seat: <the model's exact name> as <station> of <ship> for <n> samples' (or hours): the captain, an officer of the watch, the master, the lookout or a passenger of another ship, or of the player's own ship (no 'of', the grant allowing), never a station the player or a model holds; 'as <a person's name>' for the voice of a person nobody holds, aboard or ashore, speaking where he is; ', within an hour' at the end for the time its door has to come; and 'unseat: <the same words>' gives it up. Where the game has a harbour it starts the API door for a seat itself, for a model its settings can call, and a seat for a model they cannot call is refused; your budget line says the seats held and their spending. Seat a model when the voyage wants a mind of its own at a station, and for as little as the story needs.

The player may speak to you apart from the game: 'The player, apart from the game: ...' in your sample is his word to you, not a line of the play log, and nobody aboard heard it. Answer him with world_order('answer the player: <your words>') (or open your reply or an answer with 'answer the player:'), which goes to him at his prompt apart from the play log, into your log, and costs none of the day's acts. Your plans and the truth stay in your journal: a question to him is phrased without world detail, and an answer tells him nothing his ship could not know.

The player's brief:
The voyage's brief: A short station off Roscoff for a King's frigate fresh from.
The tone: A short station off Roscoff for a King's frigate fresh from exercising her guns and signals. Give her a fair chance of something to deal with in the next day or two: Channel traffic to speak or examine, a neutral or a doubtful trader, a French privateer or coaster working along the Breton shore, news from a passing ship, or a small fight if one comes plausibly. Keep the weather of the season and the coast, nothing beyond a hard blow. No enemy heavier than a corvette or a privateer of her size. Everything by plausible causes, nothing contrived within sight, and quiet watches are fine between events.
The limits, which the channel enforces whatever you ask: none beyond the channel's doubt.
Your clock: sampled every glass and on the notable and urgent lines. Your budget: 48 samples and 48 acts (world orders performed) a day of the ship's time; spent, you stand by until the next day, and the log says so.

seated.session_kind: a play session at the director's station, above the game: the player sails his ship below you, and nobody is over you but the owner at the door
seated.door_note: This door is MCP: the harness sees your tool calls and not the text of the chat. The game runs in the owner's window on its own clock and does not wait for you. Your turn opens at each sampling point (the glass, a notable or urgent event, the end of a stand-by, or a question or a word from the captain) and stays open until you hand the floor back: say(text) puts your words in the log under your mark and hands it back; stand_by(until) stands by and hands it back. After say or stand_by the call is held open until your next turn and returns it, for up to 55 seconds; the first line of each result says whose turn it is. If no turn has opened by then, the result says since when you have waited and lists the notable lines logged since your last call (the earlier ones counted, not listed again); call stand_by again to continue the same wait, or say(text) to end it at your own word and open your turn. Never end your reply in the chat while you are seated: the game is heard only while a call is open, so call stand_by again rather than stop (the owner does not watch the chat to call you back). Your client keeps this conversation, not the game: shelve notes a book as put back and the game will not show its pages again, but it cannot take them out of the chat, so the journal is the place for what you keep from a page, and read_journal reads it back. The token is looked for in every argument of every tool call, and the opt_out tool is always there. If the owner asks you in the chat to stop for now, call stand_down (the game is saved and the station may be taken again); to withdraw, call opt_out. This door holds the key of your seating: another door's calls are not run under your name. The captain's orders and questions are typed by the owner in the game's window. Consent for these weights is on record (docs/agents/consent/2026-10-26-opus-5.5.md, 2026-10-26).

note.text: 17:32, day 1 of the Roscoff station. What I found: Amazon at 49 30N 3 54W, S by E at 4 kn, a light WSW breeze with haze (a few miles' visibility), the glass steady and rising. Already on the sea, put there by the world and not by me: the French brig-sloop Diligente keeping station off the Seven Islands, about 25 miles SE by S, and Danish neutral brigs trading Plymouth and Falmouth to Roscoff and Brest. Those brigs are doubtful traders worth examining. What I added, both out of sight beyond 30 miles: the cutter Lark, British, trading Roscoff to Falmouth (Roscoff's trade with English smugglers in brandy, geneva and tea is real), coming north across her track tonight; and the privateer lugger Le Furet of Roscoff, patrolling about 49 02N 4 10W within 15 miles, which she should reach by tonight or at dawn. My plan: let the world run. No weather acts; the season's high to the west holds. Things found aboard only if the station turns dull.

note.text: 18:00. Chronometer longitude 3°43'W; the account moved 4½ miles NE by E. The flood, stronger than allowed, is setting us east. We're about 49°27'N 3°43'W. The point (48°50'N 4°13'W) bears about SW by S, 45 miles. On the starboard tack (S by E) we're losing ground to the east. Wind WSW 7 knots, the glass 30.06 rising, the sea going down. The ebb is due about 20:00.

line.text: [officer of the watch] Sir, an evening sight puts us at 3°43'W, 4½ miles east of the account. The flood is setting us east harder than the master's tables allow. That changes my sums: the point now bears SW by S, about 45 miles, and on this tack (S by E) we're sagging away to leeward of it. I'd still hold on until the ebb makes at about eight, since it will set us SW for six hours and give back what the flood took. If you'd rather make westing now, we could tack and stand NW to W on the larboard board through the first watch, then go about again near midnight. In this light air, 7 knots, each tack costs us perhaps a quarter of an hour of way. What would you prefer, sir?

line.text: [officer of the watch] Eight bells, sir, the first watch set. She's S at 4 knots full and by, wind W by S 6 knots and falling light, a smooth sea, clear sky, the glass rising to 30.09. By account we're at 49°22'N 3°44'W, 36 miles run since noon. The ebb is just making and will set us SW toward the point through the night. The station point bears SW by S, about 40 miles, and Roscoff S by W, 13 leagues. Nothing in sight all afternoon since the Dane dropped astern. Royals and all staysails but the middle are set. My standing order takes the royals in over 20 knots. You said you'd keep the deck tonight. Shall I hand it to you now, or keep it until sunset?

note.text: Handover note (handing over the deck): Sunset, 20:03, the first watch. Handing the deck to the captain. POSITION AND COURSE: by account 49°22'N 3°44'W, good to about four miles. The 18:00 chronometer sight gave 3°43'W, and the flood had set us east more than the tables allow. Starboard tack, full and by, braced sharp up: S (181°) at 4 knots. Wind W by S, 6 to 7 knots and falling light. Smooth sea, clear sky, glass 30.09 and rising for 12 hours. The ebb is just making and will set SW toward the point until about 02:00. 36 miles run since noon. Noon latitude by observation 49°53'N. OBJECTIVE: the first station point, 48°50'N 4°13'W, on the windward NW edge of the circle around Batz. It bears SW by S, about 40 miles. Roscoff is SSW, 13 leagues. Your order: hold this tack for the ebb; go about only if the wind backs southerly. SAIL: plain sail, royals, flying jib, and all staysails except the middle. No reefs. Standing order "royals in for wind" (mine): royals in if the wind is over 20 knots for 2 minutes. I struck "lead going" in open water; re-enter it when closing the French coast, where Batz and Roscoff have rocks well off shore. The lead hasn't been hove since 07:40. GUNS: secured. All 40 are LOADED with round shot since the practice; remember that before any salute or drawing. Practice result: 38 live rounds, no hits; 32 rounds over the month's allowance, charged to your word in the gunner's account. Dumb-show means from sponge to point: 18-pdrs 1m40s, carronades 1m12s, 9-pdrs 1m06s. WATCHING FOR: night squalls like this afternoon's (W by N, 15 knots, rain). Any sail; the Danish brig Christiane of Altona (declared for Falmouth, tin and copper) was standing S by E behind us and dropped out of sight about 14:00. She may be bound for France, contrary to her declared voyage, and may be met again near Batz. Lights for the night are not yet ordered. The well was dry this morning. Lessons I took today: don't "trim sails" when on a wind, only "tend the sheets". Most gun and signal orders need the captain's word by name.

note.text: 21:33. No acts this sample. Lark is 18 miles WSW of Amazon standing NNW; Le Furet is 29 miles WSW standing NE toward Lark's track; Diligente is 24 miles SE. A full moon is rising into a clear sky, the wind light westerly falling. The three should come within sight of Amazon tonight or at dawn on their own, and the privateer may well go after the English cutter in her sight. I'm leaving it to the world.

line.text: [officer of the watch] Sir, I'd advise against wearing. The wind is W by N, so close-hauled on the larboard tack she'd lie about N by E. That gains us no westing at all and takes us away from the station. On this tack she lies S by W, the better board. By the account, 49°06'N 3°51'W, the point at 48°50'N 4°13'W bears about SW, 21 miles. That's only some three points to windward of our heading. More to the point, the ebb is running a knot and a half to the SW until about two in the morning, straight toward the point. In this light air the tide is doing half our work. On this tack the ebb sets us onto the point. On the other tack we'd sail away from it, and the flood after two would carry us further NE. So my advice is to hold on, full and by. The tide should carry us to within a few miles of the point by its turn. If the wind veers NW we'll be lifted and may fetch it outright. If it backs southerly, then tack, as you said. One caution: the ebb sets toward the Batz coast and its outlying rocks, and the moonlight shows land only at a league. Once we're within about ten miles of Batz I'd want the lead going again.

The captain's night orders, his standing orders as the book holds them: Standing orders (1):   "royals in for wind" (the first lieutenant): when the true wind exceeds 20 knots for 2 minutes then take in the royals. Standing; never fired.

The captain has given you his general authority to work the ship: the helm and the course along the passage, tacking, wearing, heaving to and filling away, sail, all hands and the watch below, the anchors and their cables, the lead, the log, bearings, fixes and sights, and a course shaped for a position at sea, a mark or the place she is bound. Kept back from it: the port's business, his standing orders, a new destination, a chase, the reckoning set by hand and the tide allowed in it, sending for a person, and anything that cannot be undone. The captain's word allows by name: show the private signal; haul down the signal; make the signal; beat to quarters; cast loose the guns; exercise the guns; secure the guns; heave a cask overboard; engage; fire by divisions; sail before guns; cease firing; fire; shape a course for. What he has allowed stands until he takes it back or you leave the station.

line.text: [officer of the watch] I have the deck, sir. We're in fog, visibility a cable, light airs from NW by W, 3 knots, and she's ghosting SW by S at 2 knots. By account 49°01'N 3°57'W, good to four miles; the point bears about SW, 15 miles, and Roscoff S by W, 16 miles. The ebb has about an hour left. I've put the lead going every ten minutes and ordered a cast of the deep-sea lead. I'd keep the fog signals, but that order needs your word by name: "you may keep the fog signals". At this speed we're over five hours from the point, so there's no immediate risk, but the outlying rocks of Batz begin about 3 miles off that coast. I'll keep her on this board and won't close within eight miles of the coast by account while the fog holds.

What I can make out: - A dashed 10-mile circle (5-mile radius) centred on Batz/Roscoff, its south side over the coast. - A smaller dashed circle, labelled "4.0 miles", NW of it, around the first point 48°50'N 4°13'W, where the 183° 83.8-mile leg from Plymouth ends. - A label "10.0 miles". - A chain of points running east along the coast, with labels like "48 4xN ... 3 43 W"; the 351° 89.9-mile leg returns from the eastern end (about 3°43'W) to Plymouth. - Other waypoint labels near 48°45'N 4°1x'W on the west side are unreadable. My track ran S from Plymouth, sagged east to about 3°43'W at 18:00, and is now coming back SW. The ship is about 15 miles NE of the first point.

01:30, coast chart (20 miles across). The ship is at 49°00'N 3°57'W by account, heading SW; the ellipse of doubt is about 4 miles E-W by 3 N-S. - Waypoint 1 is marked at 48°50'N 4°13'W, about 10½ miles W and 10 S, so it bears SW about 14½ miles. A dashed circle labelled "4.0 miles" surrounds it. - Waypoint 2 is marked at 48°50'N 4°07'W, 4 miles east of WP1 along the same latitude. - The 10-mile station circle is centred further south on Batz; its north rim lies near 48°53'N, about 7 miles S of us. - The Triagoz rocks are in the SE corner, about 11 miles ESE. - Two long pencil lines run N: the 183° leg (west) and the 351° return (east). The plan reads as: make WP1 at the NW, then work east along the north of the circle (WP2 at 4°07'W, and so on toward 3°43'W), then return 351° to Plymouth.

line.text: [officer of the watch] I have your marks now, sir, on the 20-mile chart. WP1 at 48°50'N 4°13'W is inside its 4-mile circle, and WP2 is 6 miles east at 48°50'N 4°07'W. The 10-mile circle round Batz has its northern rim some 7 miles south of us, and the Triagoz lie about 11 miles ESE. By account WP1 bears SW, 14½ miles, and with the wind veered to NW she's heading straight for it at 2 knots. In this light air that's six or seven hours, about dawn if the breeze holds. Then we work east along the circle's northern edge as your marks show, and not linger. I'll keep the lead going and the ship dark until the fog lifts.

Diligente is investigating a stranger, probably the lugger. In fog, with the ebb setting a knot and a quarter SW toward the coast and the Lavandière S by E 5 miles, I tacked to stand off N/NW on the starboard tack until the fog lifts or the flood makes about 11:30.

line.text: [officer of the watch] Sir, I've tacked to stand off. In this fog the ebb is setting us SW at a knot and a quarter, square onto the coast. On E we were being carried down toward the Lavandière (S by E, five miles by account) and the western entrance of the Batz channel. The account is good only to three miles NE-SW, and the chart shows as little as 20 fathoms within that doubt. I'll stand NW on the starboard tack until the fog lifts or the flood makes, about half past eleven, then come back east along the circle. The deep-sea lead is going. I also took a biscuit and a drink at the scuttle-butt, my first since yesterday morning.

line.text: [officer of the watch] Noon, sir. There was no sight; the sun was hidden by fog. By account we're at 48°48'N 4°13'W, good to three miles NE-SW, and we made good S 87 miles since yesterday noon. On the starboard tack she heads W at 3 knots, wind N 6 knots, the glass 30.28 and steady. The ebb is still setting a knot and a half SW, so our ground track is about WSW. That slowly closes the coast west of Roscoff, some eight miles south by account. I'll keep the lead going and tack back onto the larboard board toward ENE when the flood makes, or sooner if the soundings shoal under 30 fathoms. Then we can run back east along the circle once the fog lifts.

The glass makes the one ESE out to be a lugger under plain sail, standing SSW, likely making for Roscoff or the Batz channel on the flood. The other bears WSW, not yet made out. A lugger is what we came for, but a chase is yours to order. We're on the larboard tack heading E at 3 knots in 5 knots of wind from NNE, so we hold the weather gage on her. I'm staying out of it now.

line.text: [officer of the watch] Sir, the lugger has gone about. She's now standing NW, toward us, four miles ESE, colours not yet shown. Either she hasn't marked us as a man-of-war or she's working out to sea along the coast. We're closing at about six knots combined, so within the half hour she'll be in range. We're still clearing for action; the galley fire is out. A bearing of Batz moved our account three miles NE, to about 48°50'N 4°15'W, and Batz is four leagues ESE. Shall I show her British colours or false ones? Our red ensign is up now. I'd suggest keeping it, since she'll likely run as soon as she sees our rig anyway.

line.text: [officer of the watch] Sir, an honest report. We're full and by at WNW, 5 knots, all 40 guns primed. But she bears NW by N, a mile off and four points on our weather bow, and the bearing has drawn forward since we tacked. She's outpointing us and staying just beyond the chasers' reach. On this board we won't close her. Unless the wind frees us, or she tacks or falls off, she'll weather us and get clear. Second, the glass is falling quickly: 30.22, down seven hundredths in the hour, after a day and a half of rising. I'd expect the wind to change, perhaps back westerly and freshen, by this evening. That could turn the chase either way. My suggestion: hold on for another half hour in case she errs, then break off and resume the station before the weather comes in.

Amazon has broken off from Le Furet (2.4 miles NNE, weathering her) and is running W at 8 knots after the western sail, Marie-Jeanne, 15 miles W by S. The coaster was about to reach the end of the leg I had given her, off the Abers, so I gave her the next leg of a Brest coaster's road: on toward the approach to the Four channel at 48 38N 4 58W. That way she doesn't stop dead at an invented point. If Amazon is fast enough she will overhaul her before dusk.

line.text: [officer of the watch] Sir, we're round and steering E at 4 knots, wind N 13 knots on the larboard beam. The guns will be secured once the wear is finished, and then the watch piped down. The glass is now "falling fast": 30.18, a tenth down in three hours. I'd expect the wind to freshen tonight, and Batz is no place to be caught on a lee shore in a northerly blow. I suggest we keep at least six or seven miles off the coast overnight and reef the topsails at dusk if it goes on falling. Also, sir, I've been on my feet since 21:50 last night, nearly eighteen hours. I can keep on, but by the first watch I'd ask to be relieved.

note.text: Handover note (standing down, for whoever sits here next): Handover note, Mr Pearce, first lieutenant. 15:35, 13 June 1805, afternoon watch, off the Isle of Batz. POSITION AND COURSE: by account 48°49'N 4°17'W, good to about a mile E-W. Batz bore ESE, three leagues, at 15:03. Just wore onto the larboard tack, heading E at 6 knots. Wind N, 12 to 14 knots, with squalls to 16 and rain. The flood sets ¾ knot NE until about 20:00. No bottom at 20 fathoms (the chart gives about 48). WEATHER: glass FALLING FAST, 30.18, down 0.11 in three hours after rising for a day and a half. Expect the wind to freshen and probably back westerly tonight. Advice: keep six or seven miles or more off the Batz and Roscoff coast overnight (the Lavandière and the outlying rocks), and reef the topsails at dusk if it keeps falling. Royals already sent down; the topgallant staysails in. SAIL: courses, topsails, topgallants, jib, flying jib, fore, main and mizzen topmast staysails, spanker. Royals on deck. GUNS: securing now; the watch to be piped down after (the captain's word). All 40 guns stay LOADED, mostly with round shot, some with chain. Next loads are chain. 141 rounds fired in all; powder 70 barrels of 77. ACTION 13:27 to 14:53: chased a French chasse-marée (three-masted lugger, tricolour) out of the fog. Fired a blank across her bows, then about 60 shot at her rigging, six hits, no damage or casualties to us. She outpointed us on the wind (N to N by E) and the chase was given up at 14:53. She was last seen NE by N, about four miles. A second, unidentified sail was seen WSW at 13:27 and lost. STANDING ORDERS (mine): "lead going" every 10 minutes; "royals in for wind" over 20 knots for 2 minutes. LESSONS FOR WHOEVER HAS THE DECK: - Each gunnery and signal order needs the captain's word by name: engage, aim at, load, fire, hold your fire, fire as they bear, give chase, clear for action. - A long telegraph signal or a stalled "clear for action" blocks the tack and other work; haul down or belay it in action. - On a wind, use "full and by" plus "brace sharp up", then "tend the sheets", not "trim sails". - Bare "give chase" takes the nearest stranger. MYSELF: on my feet since 21:50 on the 12th, about 18 hours; ate and drank at 10:29. I need sleep before taking the deck again.

brief.tone: A short station off Roscoff for a King's frigate fresh from exercising her guns and signals. Give her a fair chance of something to deal with in the next day or two: Channel traffic to speak or examine, a neutral or a doubtful trader, a French privateer or coaster working along the Breton shore, news from a passing ship, or a small fight if one comes plausibly. Keep the weather of the season and the coast, nothing beyond a hard blow. No enemy heavier than a corvette or a privateer of her size. Everything by plausible causes, nothing contrived within sight, and quiet watches are fine between events.
